```json
{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "Unit economics: B's sourced price anchors are $15-45 per agent per month (CrankWheel $29 Solo, Blitzz $15-45 per agent). A's anchor is Lody at $8-10 per seat, with a sourced devtools cost per SQL of about $650. That means A has to win multi-seat team deals just to recover acquisition cost, which is hard to reach within 90 days.",
    "Channel: B names a concrete, budget-primed channel. Zendesk Marketplace buyers already expect to pay $500-$5,000+ per year for add-ons, and there is no listing fee. A offers only a Product Hunt launch costing $3,300-$6,000 of founder time, plus expensive devtools search ads.",
    "Free substitutes: A's free substitute is Slack Code, from a major incumbent (Salesforce) and bundled into every Slack plan. That sets a $0 anchor inside the tool the target buyer already uses, and A faces at least five direct competitors that launched in the same window. B's free substitutes (Quick Assist, JoinByKey) are real, but they are consumer and ad-hoc tools that do not sit inside a support team's workflow. That leaves a more plausible wedge for small support teams.",
    "Unsourced load-bearing claims: two of A's key claims are marked [unsourced], namely solo buildability in six weeks and demand outside engineering. Under the rules these count as missing. B's buildability claim rests on a sourced existence proof (JoinByKey).",
    "B's own weaknesses are real. Its demand quotes come from family caregivers rather than support-team buyers, and compliance (SOC2, HIPAA) may gate regulated verticals. A, however, carries the same compliance burden (SOC2, ZDR, SSO) at a lower price point and with fiercer competition."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "A's demand evidence is two quotes from blog posts (agentcenter.cloud and dev.to). Neither shows a buyer willing to pay for a multiplayer agent workspace. The agentcenter quote, attributed to an operations lead, appears to come from a vendor's content marketing. A instead leans on competitor convergence and a YC Fall 2026 RFS as demand signals. The RFS has no URL, and competitor convergence shows perceived opportunity, not proven willingness to pay.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate to low confidence. Neither brief contains direct evidence of a paying B2B buyer. B's demand quotes are from consumers, which mismatches its stated payer, and A's are generic pain statements. B wins mainly on higher per-seat pricing, a concrete marketplace channel, and the absence of a free bundled incumbent offering inside the buyer's existing workflow. It does not win on stronger demand proof."
}
```
